hints: Start by picturing meiosis I - when do homologous chromosomes pair up together, and when do they line up to be pulled apart?
Focus first on prophase I - what happens when non-sister chromatids of a paired homologous pair touch and swap sections?
Think about the name for those X-shaped contact points and what exactly is exchanged - DNA or whole chromosomes?
Link that exchange to alleles - how does swapping create chromatids with a new mix that breaks old linkage groups?
Now move to metaphase I - if maternal and paternal homologues line up randomly, how many ways can the pairs face the poles?
Recall the formula for that shuffling and why it gives a huge number of different gametes even without any swapping.
Do not forget meiosis II - what else assorts independently when sister chromatids line up in metaphase II?
Add one final distinct source of new variation that can occur at any time during DNA replication before or during meiosis.
walkthrough:
Crossing Over in Prophase I Creates Recombinant Chromatids**
You and I know homologous chromosomes carry the same genes but often different alleles - one maternal, one paternal. In prophase I they pair up closely. At points called chiasmata, non-sister chromatids break and rejoin, a process called crossing over. This is a physical exchange of genetic material, not whole chromosomes.

Why That Matters - New Allele Mixes**
Because alleles are swapped, each chromatid now carries a new combination of alleles that neither parent chromosome had. Genes that were linked together on the same chromosome can be separated, so linkage groups are broken. That alone makes four chromatids in each bivalent genetically different.

Independent Assortment Multiplies the Variation**
Now think about lining up. In metaphase I, each bivalent lines up randomly - maternal homologue to one pole or the other, independently of all other pairs. With n pairs, that gives $2^n$ possible chromosome combinations in the daughter cells. In metaphase II, sister chromatids, which are now non-identical because of crossing over, also assort independently. Together these two shuffles produce a very large number of genetically different gametes. Random mutation adds further new alleles.

Final answer: In prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair and chiasmata form with crossing over between non-sister chromatids, exchanging genetic material to give new combinations of alleles and break linkage groups. In metaphase I, homologous pairs / bivalents assort independently / randomly, giving $2^n$ combinations. In metaphase II, chromatids / chromosomes assort independently. Mutation also creates new variation.

hints: Start with the central idea - genes code for proteins, so what kind of protein would a pigment gene normally make?
Recall the specific gene and enzyme here - the TYR gene and its product tyrosinase found in melanocytes.
Trace the normal pathway - what starting molecule does tyrosinase act on and what intermediates are formed?
Link that pathway to the visible outcome - what final pigment is made and where in the body does it appear?
Now think about inheritance - is the albinism allele dominant or recessive, and what does that tell you about carriers?
Consider what the mutation does to the protein - why would the enzyme be missing or fail to work?
Put it together - why does only one genotype show no pigment in hair, skin and irises?
walkthrough:
Normal Gene to Normal Enzyme to Normal Pigment**
Think gene to protein to trait. The normal TYR gene is transcribed and translated in special cells called melanocytes to make the enzyme tyrosinase. Tyrosinase catalyses conversion of the amino acid tyrosine to DOPA then to dopaquinone, which is then converted to melanin. Melanin is the pigment that colours hair, skin and irises.

Mutant Allele Means Broken Enzyme**
A mutation in TYR changes the base sequence so the coded protein is altered. The mutant allele produces either no tyrosinase or an inactive enzyme with a wrong shape that cannot bind tyrosine. Without working tyrosinase, the whole pathway stops and no melanin is made, so the opposite outcome occurs.

Why It Is Recessive and Only Shows in Homozygotes**
The mutant albinism allele is recessive. A heterozygote still has one normal TYR allele making enough functional tyrosinase to make melanin, so they have normal pigmentation. Only homozygous recessive people have no functional copy, so they make no melanin and show albinism in hair, skin and eyes.

Final answer: Normal TYR gene codes for enzyme tyrosinase in melanocytes. Tyrosinase converts tyrosine to DOPA / dopaquinone to form melanin pigment in hair, skin and irises. Mutant allele is recessive and codes for no / inactive tyrosinase, so no melanin is made. Only homozygous recessive individuals show albinism.
